DDCL-INCRT: A Self-Organising Transformer with Hierarchical Prototype Structure
(Theoretical Foundations)

Giansalvo Cirrincione Email: exin@u-picardie.fr Affiliation: Laboratory LTI, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, Chemin du Thil, Amiens, 80025, France
Abstract

Modern neural networks of the transformer family [4] require the practitioner to decide, before any training begins, how many attention heads to use, how deep the network should be, and how wide each component should be. These decisions are made without knowledge of the task, and the result is invariably an architecture that is larger than necessary: empirical studies consistently find that a substantial fraction of the heads and layers can be removed after training without any loss in performance [5, 6, 7].

This paper introduces DDCL-INCRT, an architecture that solves this problem by determining its own structure during training. The approach is built on two complementary ideas. The first, called DDCL (Deep Dual Competitive Learning) [1], replaces the standard feedforward block of each transformer layer with a small dictionary of learned prototype vectors that represent the most informative directions in the data. The dictionary is self-organising: the prototypes spread apart automatically, driven by the mathematics of the training objective, without any need for explicit regularisation. The second, called INCRT (Incremental Transformer) [3], controls how many heads the network should have. It starts from a single head and adds a new one only when a measurable criterion, namely the amount of directional information that the current heads fail to capture, exceeds a threshold. When the criterion falls below the threshold, growth stops.

The main theoretical finding is that these two ideas reinforce each other in a precise mathematical sense: each time a new head is added, the separation between prototypes increases, and the increased separation in turn raises the signal that may trigger the next addition. At convergence, the network has organised itself into a hierarchy of heads ordered by the granularity of the information they represent, from fine-grained local patterns to coarse-grained global ones. The paper proves that this hierarchical structure is unique and minimal: it is the smallest architecture that is sufficient for the task, and it is the same regardless of the random initialisation, under the conditions stated in the theorems. Formal guarantees of stability, convergence, and robustness to pruning are established throughout.

The architecture is not something one designs. It is something one derives.

Keywords: 
competitive learning , hierarchical prototype structure , incremental architecture , prototype learning , self-determining transformer , stability analysis

1 Introduction

1.1 The problem: transformers do not know how large they should be

A transformer neural network [4] is assembled from decisions made before training begins. How many attention heads? How many layers? How wide should the feedforward block be? None of these questions has a principled answer grounded in the properties of the task. In practice they are resolved by grid search, intuition, or scaling laws that describe trends without explaining mechanisms [8]. The resulting architectures are then trained, compressed, and analysed, in that order.

The empirical evidence that this process systematically over-specifies the architecture is now substantial. A small number of functionally specialised heads carry the bulk of the predictive load in a trained transformer, while the majority can be removed without performance loss [5, 6]. Up to 50% of attention layers in large language models can be dropped after training without degrading performance [7].

Why is this redundancy so systematic? The answer lies in a structural property of the standard transformer. Each attention head computes a representation of how tokens in a sequence relate to each other: some tokens attend strongly to others, some weakly, and the pattern of these relationships encodes information about the structure of the input. Part of this relational information is symmetric (token AA attends to token BB as much as BB attends to AA), and part is asymmetric (the flow of attention is directional, from one token toward another). The asymmetric, or directional, component is particularly important because it is the only part that can encode ordered relationships, such as grammatical dependencies or causal structure. The feedforward block that follows each attention layer processes the output using a fixed random basis, its weight matrices, which captures the dominant directional component only partially and at random. The formal consequence, proved in [2] as the Channel Destruction Theorem, is that the feedforward block systematically discards the directional information computed by the attention. The architecture must compensate for this loss by adding more heads, heads that would not be needed if the information were preserved. Redundancy is thus not a failure of architecture search. It is the inevitable consequence of using a fixed, randomly initialised block to process an adaptively computed signal.

1.2 The approach: a self-organising prototype layer

The architecture studied in this paper eliminates redundancy by construction. The feedforward block at each transformer layer is replaced by a competitive prototype layer whose basis is not fixed but learned, and whose number of heads grows during training to cover exactly the directional information that the attention computes.

Two building blocks are required.

The prototype layer (DDCL).

Deep Dual Competitive Learning [1] replaces the feedforward block with a bank of KK prototype vectors in the embedding space. Each input token is assigned to the prototypes via a soft nearest-neighbour rule: the assignment weight of token nn to prototype kk is large when the token is geometrically close to the prototype and small otherwise. The layer output for each token is then the weighted average of the prototypes, with weights given by these proximity-based assignments.

This replacement has a non-obvious algebraic consequence. The training loss, which measures how well the prototypes cover the token distribution, decomposes exactly into two terms: a clustering fidelity term and a separation term that is always non-negative. The gradient of the separation term pushes the prototypes apart whenever any two of them coincide, which means that prototype collapse is a first-order unstable equilibrium of the loss. The prototypes spread apart automatically, driven by the mathematics of the objective, without any explicit regularisation. Crucially, the entire layer is end-to-end differentiable. Standard feedforward blocks transform the input through weight matrices to produce an output. The DCL layer inverts this logic: it transposes the role of input and output, so that the prototypes themselves are the output of the layer, selected and combined by the assignment weights. Because the output is a smooth, differentiable function of the assignment weights, gradients flow freely back through the layer to the encoder, with no need for the straight-through estimators or other approximations required by vector-quantisation methods [17].

The growth mechanism (INCRT).

The Incremental Transformer [3] addresses a separate question: how many prototype heads should there be? The architecture starts from a single head and adds a new one only when a measurable criterion indicates that the current heads are insufficient.

The insufficiency criterion is based on the notion of residual directional content. After KK heads have been added, each covering a certain pattern of directional relationships between tokens, some directional content in the attention signal remains uncovered. Formally, this residual is measured by projecting the attention signal onto the subspace that is orthogonal to all directions already captured by the existing heads, and computing the dominant eigenvalue of the resulting matrix. When this eigenvalue exceeds a threshold θw\theta_{w}, there is still significant directional content that the current heads do not represent, and a new head is added in the direction of maximum residual content. When the eigenvalue falls below θw\theta_{w}, the architecture has captured enough and growth stops. The final number of heads is determined entirely by the structure of the attention signal on the training data, not by any hyperparameter set in advance.

The integration and its central consequence.

DDCL-INCRT combines these two building blocks at each transformer layer. The feedforward block is replaced by a DDCL prototype layer whose heads are grown and pruned by the INCRT mechanism. Each new head is initialised in the direction of maximum residual directional content at the moment of its birth, and the growth criterion is re-evaluated after each prototype update.

The natural question is whether these two mechanisms interact cleanly. DDCL operates on the assignment distribution of tokens to prototypes. INCRT operates on the residual directional content of the attention signal. These are genuinely different objects, computed from different parts of the architecture.

The answer proved in this paper is that they are mutually reinforcing. Each growth step triggered by INCRT amplifies the separation force that DDCL exerts on the prototypes, because the new head is born in the direction of maximum residual content, precisely the direction in which the prototypes have the most room to separate. The separation of the prototypes in turn raises the residual directional content that will trigger the next growth step, because well-separated prototypes span a larger subspace, leaving more content for the attention signal to find. The two mechanisms form a self-reinforcing cycle that drives the architecture toward the unique minimal structure sufficient for the task.

1.3 Contributions

The contributions of this paper are organised in three groups.

Training dynamics of the integrated layer. It is proved that each growth step amplifies the prototype separation force by a gain that depends on the dominant eigenvalue of the residual matrix and the current temperature of the prototype assignments (Theorem 2). It is also proved that trainable per-head temperatures spontaneously partition the heads into two groups: heads that converge to hard, discrete prototype assignments (local heads), and heads that maintain soft, continuous centroid representations (global heads). This partition is determined by the spectral structure of the attention signal, not by any architectural choice (Theorem 3). Finally, it is proved that replacing the feedforward block with the DDCL-INCRT layer strictly reduces the directional information lost at every transformer layer, almost surely under standard weight initialisation (Theorem 4).

Global well-behavedness. A piecewise free energy functional is constructed that is non-increasing across all growth events, pruning events, and training steps, constituting a global Lyapunov function for the full system, comprising encoder weights, prototype banks, and temperatures, with a growing architecture (Theorem 8). This closes an open problem stated in [2]. The architecture is proved to converge to a minimal sufficient configuration in finitely many growth steps, almost surely (Theorem 5). It is also shown that pruning a head cannot collapse the prototypes of the surviving heads, and that the separation force on surviving heads is non-decreasing after pruning (Theorem 6). All results extend to discrete-time stochastic gradient descent under an explicit step-size condition (Theorem 7).

The architecture at convergence. The structure that emerges when training stops is characterised. The heads are ordered by the amount of directional content they cover: the first head added covers the largest portion, the second covers the next, and so on. The prototype separation force is strictly larger in heads that cover finer-grained directional content. The resulting hierarchy is the minimally sufficient structure for the task, and it is the same regardless of the random initialisation (Theorem 10).

A single co-emergence theorem (Corollary 14) states all seven properties as simultaneous consequences of one geometric principle: structure emerges from measurable insufficiency.

Scope. This is a theoretical paper. The experimental section provides numerical illustrations of the main theoretical predictions on synthetic and real data. Its purpose is to verify that the quantities predicted by the theory, namely separation force amplification, temperature specialisation, spectral ordering, and pruning safety, behave as the theorems state, not to demonstrate competitive performance on standard benchmarks. Empirical evaluation on large-scale NLP tasks is the subject of ongoing work.

1.4 How to read this paper

Section 2 places the work in the context of the existing literature on transformer compression, adaptive architectures, and prototype learning. Section 3 defines the notation and the two building blocks precisely and from scratch, assuming only familiarity with transformer self-attention. No prior knowledge of the DDCL or INCRT papers is required: all definitions and results used from those papers are restated here in full. Parts I–III develop the theoretical contributions in order. Section 7 provides numerical illustrations of the main predictions on synthetic data and on BERT embeddings. Section 13 situates the results in the broader context of architecture design and identifies open directions.

2 Related Work

2.1 Transformer redundancy and attention head analysis

The redundancy of transformer architectures has been documented from multiple angles. At the level of attention heads, it has been shown that the vast majority of heads in a trained transformer are functionally dispensable: removing them causes negligible degradation on downstream tasks, while a small subset of specialised heads carries most of the predictive load [5, 6]. At the level of layers, up to half of the attention layers in large language models can be dropped after training without significant performance loss [7]. These findings are not coincidental: as proved in the DDCL-Attention paper [2], they follow from a structural property of the standard architecture. The feedforward block that follows each attention layer processes the attention output through a fixed random basis, which systematically discards the directional ordering information computed by the attention mechanism. The architecture compensates by adding heads, most of which are therefore redundant by construction.

2.2 Pruning and compression

The predominant response to transformer redundancy has been post-hoc compression: train a large model, then reduce it. Magnitude-based weight pruning [9] and the lottery ticket hypothesis [10] established the general principle that sparse subnetworks with full performance exist within over-parametrised models. Applied to transformers, structured pruning methods remove entire attention heads [5, 6] or layers [7] based on importance scores computed from gradients, Taylor expansions, or attention entropy. Knowledge distillation offers a complementary route [11]: a large teacher model is trained first, and its knowledge is transferred to a smaller student, as in DistilBERT [12] and TinyBERT [30].

All of these methods share a common limitation: the redundant capacity is trained before it is removed. This wastes computation during training and can introduce instabilities when the pruned heads carried inter-dependent representations. DDCL-INCRT addresses the redundancy before it arises, by growing the architecture only as far as the task requires.

2.3 Adaptive computation and growing architectures

A smaller body of work has explored the opposite direction: starting small and growing during training. Net2Net [13] introduced function-preserving transformations for widening and deepening networks, enabling knowledge transfer from smaller to larger models. Progressive stacking [14] grows transformers by duplicating layers, achieving faster convergence on language modelling tasks. The Firefly framework [34] grows networks by steepest descent in a functional neighbourhood, selecting the best structural extension at each step via a greedy Taylor approximation. Neural Architecture Search [15, 16] optimises over discrete architecture spaces jointly with weights, at the cost of substantial computational overhead and without formal convergence guarantees.

These methods share the goal of avoiding over-parametrisation, but differ fundamentally from DDCL-INCRT in two respects. First, the growth criterion is either heuristic (layer duplication, Taylor approximation) or based on a global search (NAS), rather than derived from a mathematically characterised property of the signal the architecture processes. Second, none of these methods provides formal guarantees that the final architecture is minimally sufficient: the growth may stop too early or too late depending on hyperparameters. The INCRT growth criterion is provably equivalent to a greedy Rayleigh quotient optimisation on the residual directional content [3], giving a stopping condition whose sufficiency is theoretically characterised.

2.4 Competitive learning and prototype methods

Competitive learning, in which a set of prototype vectors compete to represent the input, has a long history in unsupervised learning [31]. Modern deep variants include vector-quantised autoencoders (VQ-VAE [17]), which learn a discrete codebook via a straight-through estimator, and Slot Attention [18], which iteratively refines a fixed number of slots via a GRU to segment visual scenes. Prototypical networks [19] use per-class centroids for few-shot classification, and prototypical contrastive learning [32] incorporates prototype anchors into a contrastive objective.

DDCL [1] differs from all of these in a structurally important way. In VQ-VAE, the discrete assignment step is non-differentiable and requires a straight-through estimator to allow gradient flow. In Slot Attention, the slot update requires multiple GRU iterations at inference time. In DDCL, the output of the layer is a weighted combination of the prototype vectors, selected by soft assignment weights. Because the output is a smooth, differentiable function of these weights, gradients flow freely back through the layer to the encoder without approximation. Furthermore, the DDCL training loss admits an exact algebraic decomposition into a clustering fidelity term and a non-negative separation term whose gradient always pushes prototypes apart, providing an explicit anti-collapse force that is absent from VQ-VAE and Slot Attention. This decomposition is derived formally in Section 3.

2.5 Hierarchical representation learning

The idea that useful representations are naturally hierarchical has motivated a wide range of architectures, from classical agglomerative clustering [20] to deep generative models. Capsule networks [21] explicitly model part-whole relationships via dynamic routing between layers of capsules. Hierarchical VAEs [22] learn multi-scale latent representations by stacking variational layers. The connection to the feature-learning regime of neural networks has been formalised by Roberts et al. [23], who show that the depth-to-width ratio governs the transition between kernel and feature learning.

DDCL-INCRT produces a hierarchy by a different mechanism: the heads are not placed at different levels of a fixed architecture, but grow in order of the directional content they cover. The hierarchy is therefore a property of the task data, not of the architecture design. The uniqueness of the resulting hierarchy (Theorem 10) has no analogue in the capsule or hierarchical VAE literature, where the number of levels and the routing mechanism are architectural choices.

2.6 Stability theory and stochastic approximation

The analysis of learning systems via Lyapunov functions is classical [27], and the two-timescale stochastic approximation framework of Borkar [28] provides the standard toolkit for coupled gradient systems. The singular perturbation approach of Tikhonov [24], extended to infinite intervals by Hoppensteadt [29] and Kokotovic et al. [25], provides the continuous-time analogue.

Applied to deep learning, stability results for prototype learning systems have been established in [1] for the frozen-encoder case and extended to the full coupled encoder-prototype system in [2] via a free-energy Lyapunov argument. The present paper extends these results further to the growing-architecture setting, where the system is hybrid: continuous dynamics on dwell intervals, discrete jumps at growth and pruning events. The construction of a piecewise Lyapunov function that is non-increasing across both the continuous and discrete components is, to our knowledge, novel in the context of adaptive transformer architectures.

Part I: The DDCL-INCRT Layer

This part defines the DDCL-INCRT layer, establishes notation, and proves three properties of its training dynamics: mutual reinforcement between the competitive learning objective and the growth criterion (Section 4), spontaneous temperature specialisation into local and global prototype regimes (Section 5), and strict dominance over the standard MLP block in terms of directional information preservation (Section 6).

3 Setup and Notation

Table of assumptions

Table 2 lists all assumptions used in this paper. Although the list is long, the assumptions fall into three natural groups and are all standard or practically verifiable. The regularity conditions (A1)–(A3) and (B1)–(B3) are mild non-degeneracy requirements that hold generically and are satisfied by default under random initialisation. The step-size conditions (E1)–(E6) reduce to the simple three-timescale rule ηT≪ηP≪η+\eta_{T}\ll\eta_{P}\ll\eta^{+} (Corollary 9), which is easy to enforce in practice. The structural conditions (F1)–(F2) and (H1)–(H5) are standard in the stochastic approximation and competitive learning literature and are inherited from the prior DDCL and INCRT frameworks. No assumption requires knowledge of the task or the data distribution in advance.

3.1 The DDCL prototype layer

Consider a sequence of NN input tokens, represented as vectors z1,…,zN∈ℝmz_{1},\ldots,z_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} produced by a differentiable encoder fθf_{\theta}. The encoder maps each input xnx_{n} to an embedding zn=fθ​(xn)z_{n}=f_{\theta}(x_{n}); the collection of all embeddings is denoted Z={zn}n=1NZ=\{z_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}.

The DDCL layer maintains a bank of KK prototype vectors P={p1,…,pK}⊂ℝmP=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{K}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{m}. Each token znz_{n} is assigned to the prototypes via a soft nearest-neighbour rule: the assignment weight of token nn to prototype kk, denoted qn​kq_{nk}, is computed as a softmax over negative squared distances,

qn​k=exp(−∥zn−pk∥2/T)∑k′exp(−∥zn−pk′∥2/T),q_{nk}=\frac{\exp(-\|z_{n}-p_{k}\|^{2}/T)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k^{\prime}}\exp(-\|z_{n}-p_{k^{\prime}}\|^{2}/T)}, (1)

where T>0T>0 is a temperature parameter that controls how sharply the assignments concentrate on the nearest prototype. The output of the layer for token nn is the soft centroid μn=∑kqn​k​pk\mu_{n}=\sum_{k}q_{nk}\,p_{k}, a weighted average of the prototypes.

The training loss is the expected squared distance of each token from its soft centroid. Letting NN denote the number of tokens and KK the number of prototypes, it is defined as:

ℒq=∑n=1N∑k=1Kqn​k​‖zn−pk‖2.\mathcal{L}_{q}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{nk}\,\|z_{n}-p_{k}\|^{2}. (2)

This loss admits an exact algebraic decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V, where LOLS=∑nmink⁡‖zn−pk‖2L_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\sum_{n}\min_{k}\|z_{n}-p_{k}\|^{2} measures clustering fidelity (how well the nearest prototype covers each token), and V=∑n∑kqn​k​‖pk−μn‖2≥0V=\sum_{n}\sum_{k}q_{nk}\|p_{k}-\mu_{n}\|^{2}\geq 0 is a separation term. The gradient of VV with respect to the prototypes is ∇PV=2​P​Σq\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q}, where Σq=∑n(diag⁡(qn)−qn​qn⊤)\Sigma_{q}=\sum_{n}(\mathrm{diag}(q_{n})-q_{n}q_{n}^{\top}) is the aggregated soft assignment covariance matrix, which is always positive semidefinite. This gradient acts as a separation force: whenever two prototypes coincide, it pushes them apart.

3.2 The INCRT growth criterion

The INCRT mechanism operates on the attention weight product. For a single attention head, the weight matrices WQW_{Q} and WKW_{K} produce a product M=WQ​WK⊤M=W_{Q}W_{K}^{\top} that governs which tokens attend to which. This product decomposes as M=Ms+MaM=M_{s}+M_{a}, where Ms=(M+M⊤)/2M_{s}=(M+M^{\top})/2 is the symmetric part (governing reciprocal attention) and Ma=(M−M⊤)/2M_{a}=(M-M^{\top})/2 is the antisymmetric part, which is the unique source of directed, asymmetric information flow between tokens.

After KK heads have been added at layer ll, each covering a certain subspace of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the directions not yet covered form the residual subspace. Let Q(l)∈ℝd×KQ^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} be the orthonormal basis of directions already captured, and let P⟂=I−Q(l)​Q(l)⊤P^{\perp}=I-Q^{(l)}Q^{(l)\top} be the projector onto the residual subspace. The residual matrix is defined as:

Ares(l)=P⟂​X​Ma​X⊤​P⟂,A_{\rm res}^{(l)}=P^{\perp}\,XM_{a}X^{\top}P^{\perp}, (3)

where X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} collects the input token representations. The largest eigenvalue of Ares(l)A_{\rm res}^{(l)}, denoted λmax​(Ares(l))\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}), measures how much directional content remains uncaptured. The INCRT growth criterion adds a new head in the direction of the dominant eigenvector v1​(Ares(K))v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)}) whenever λmax​(Ares(K))>θw\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)})>\theta_{w}, and stops growing when this eigenvalue falls below the threshold θw\theta_{w}.

The subspace captured by the KK heads grown so far is 𝒱(K)=span⁡{u1+,…,uK+}\mathcal{V}^{(K)}=\mathrm{span}\{u_{1}^{+},\ldots,u_{K}^{+}\}, where uh+u_{h}^{+} denotes the direction added at growth step hh. The separation force magnitude, which measures the strength of the anti-collapse force exerted by the prototype bank, is defined as:

Fsep​(P,Z)=‖∇PV‖F2=4​∑k=1K‖∑n=1Nqn​k​(pk−μn)‖2.F_{\rm sep}(P,Z)=\|\nabla_{P}V\|_{F}^{2}=4\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Bigl\|\sum_{n=1}^{N}q_{nk}(p_{k}-\mu_{n})\Bigr\|^{2}. (4)

3.4 The DDCL-INCRT integration

The two mechanisms interact within each training iteration in a mutually reinforcing cycle. The DDCL prototype updates (Step 2) spread the prototypes across the embedding space, which changes the effective coverage of the existing heads and raises the residual directional content measured by AresA_{\rm res}. The INCRT growth step (Step 3), when triggered, adds a new head whose prototypes are born in the direction of maximum residual content, immediately amplifying the separation force on those prototypes. The algorithm below makes this cycle explicit.

4 Mutual Reinforcement of the DDCL and INCRT Dynamics

The first question about the DDCL-INCRT integration is whether the two mechanisms are compatible at all. Could the growth steps triggered by INCRT disrupt the prototype organisation built up by DDCL? The answer proved in this section is the opposite: every growth step not only preserves the separation force on the existing prototypes but strictly amplifies it.

To understand why, recall that when INCRT adds a new head, the prototypes of that head are initialised along the direction u∗u^{*} of maximum residual content in the attention signal. This is precisely the direction in which the token embeddings have the most variance not yet captured by the existing heads. Projecting the tokens onto this new direction increases the effective spread of the embeddings, which in turn increases the distances between soft centroids and prototypes, the very quantity that drives the separation force. The net effect is a strict amplification of FsepF_{\rm sep}, with a gain that scales with the magnitude of the residual signal λmax​(Ares)\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}) and decreases with the temperature TT (higher temperature means softer assignments and a weaker separation force).

The proof proceeds in three steps: an algebraic analysis of the assignment covariance matrix Σq\Sigma_{q} (Lemma 1), a first-order perturbation argument showing that FsepF_{\rm sep} is non-decreasing (Theorem 1), and a second-order analysis that quantifies the strict gain (Theorem 2).

Lemma 2 (First-order variation of Σq\Sigma_{q}).

dd​ϵ|ϵ=0​tr​(Σq)=2T​∑n∑kqn​k​(1−2​qn​k)​⟨𝝁n−𝐩k,u∗⟩​αn.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\bigg|_{\epsilon=0}\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q})=\frac{2}{T}\sum_{n}\sum_{k}q_{nk}(1-2q_{nk})\langle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k},u^{*}\rangle\alpha_{n}. (5)
Proof.

By direct differentiation of qn​kq_{nk} with respect to 𝐳n\mathbf{z}_{n} under the softmax structure: ∂qn​k/∂𝐳n=(2/T)​qn​k​(𝝁n−𝐩k)\partial q_{nk}/\partial\mathbf{z}_{n}=(2/T)q_{nk}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}). Differentiating H2​(𝐪n)H_{2}(\mathbf{q}_{n}) via the chain rule and summing over nn yields the result. ∎

Lemma 3 (First-order variation of assignment weights).

Denote by pk∗=⟨pk,u∗⟩p_{k}^{*}=\langle p_{k},u^{*}\rangle the projection of prototype kk onto u∗u^{*}, and by p¯n∗=∑kqn​k​pk∗\bar{p}_{n}^{*}=\sum_{k}q_{nk}p_{k}^{*} the corresponding soft centroid projection. Under the same perturbation:

q˙n​k≡d​qn​kd​ϵ|ϵ=0=2​αnT​qn​k​(pk∗−p¯n∗).\dot{q}_{nk}\equiv\frac{dq_{nk}}{d\epsilon}\bigg|_{\epsilon=0}=\frac{2\alpha_{n}}{T}\,q_{nk}\,(p_{k}^{*}-\bar{p}_{n}^{*}). (6)

From the softmax formula, ∂qn​k/∂𝐳n=(2/T)​qn​k​(𝝁n−𝐩k)\partial q_{nk}/\partial\mathbf{z}_{n}=(2/T)q_{nk}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}). Projecting onto u∗u^{*} and noting ⟨𝝁n−𝐩k,u∗⟩=p¯n∗−pk∗\langle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k},u^{*}\rangle=\bar{p}_{n}^{*}-p_{k}^{*} gives (6). ∎

Lemma 4 (Sign of the residual-covariance term).

Let u∗=v1​(Ares(K))u^{*}=v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)}), αn=⟨zn,u∗⟩\alpha_{n}=\langle z_{n},u^{*}\rangle, and pk∗=⟨pk,u∗⟩p_{k}^{*}=\langle p_{k},u^{*}\rangle. Define the empirical covariance

Ck≜∑nαn​(pk∗−p¯n∗).C_{k}\;\triangleq\;\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\,(p_{k}^{*}-\bar{p}_{n}^{*}). (7)

Under (A2’), Ck≥0C_{k}\geq 0 for all kk, with Ck>0C_{k}>0 for at least one kk.

Proof.

Write sk≜pk∗−p¯n∗s_{k}\triangleq p_{k}^{*}-\bar{p}_{n}^{*} for the deviation of prototype kk’s projection from the soft-centroid projection at token nn. Since p¯n∗=∑k′qn​k′​pk′∗\bar{p}_{n}^{*}=\sum_{k^{\prime}}q_{nk^{\prime}}p_{k^{\prime}}^{*} is the qnq_{n}-weighted average of {pk′∗}\{p_{k^{\prime}}^{*}\}, we have ∑kqn​k​sk=0\sum_{k}q_{nk}s_{k}=0 for every nn (the deviations sum to zero under any probability vector qnq_{n}).

Now αn=⟨zn,u∗⟩\alpha_{n}=\langle z_{n},u^{*}\rangle measures how far token nn projects onto u∗u^{*}. Tokens with large |αn||\alpha_{n}| are farthest from the origin in the direction of maximum residual variance. By the soft nearest-neighbour rule, such tokens concentrate their assignment weight on the prototype kn∗=arg⁡maxk⁡pk∗k^{*}_{n}=\arg\max_{k}p_{k}^{*} if αn>0\alpha_{n}>0, or on arg⁡mink⁡pk∗\arg\min_{k}p_{k}^{*} if αn<0\alpha_{n}<0. In either case the dominant term in Ck=∑nαn​skC_{k}=\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}s_{k} pairs large |αn||\alpha_{n}| with the matching sign of sks_{k}, giving a non-negative contribution.

More formally, decompose

Ck=∑nαn​pk∗−∑nαn​p¯n∗=pk∗​A−Bk,C_{k}=\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}p_{k}^{*}-\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\bar{p}_{n}^{*}=p_{k}^{*}A-B_{k}, (8)

Since u∗=v1​(Ares(K))u^{*}=v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)}) lies in the residual subspace orthogonal to all previously captured directions, and the token embeddings znz_{n} have zero mean in that subspace (they are centred), we have A=∑n⟨zn,u∗⟩=0A=\sum_{n}\langle z_{n},u^{*}\rangle=0. Therefore Ck=−Bk=−∑nαnp¯n∗=−∑nαn∑k′qn​k′pk′∗C_{k}=-B_{k}=-\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\bar{p}_{n}^{*}=-\sum_{n}\alpha_{n}\sum_{k^{\prime}}q_{nk^{\prime}}p_{k^{\prime}}^{*}.

Substituting and rearranging:

where 𝐆k​k′=∑nqn​k′​pk′∗\mathbf{G}_{kk^{\prime}}=\sum_{n}q_{nk^{\prime}}p_{k^{\prime}}^{*} and 𝐫k=∑nqn​k​(pk−μn)\mathbf{r}_{k}=\sum_{n}q_{nk}(p_{k}-\mu_{n}) is the residual force of prototype kk. Under (A1), 𝐫k≠0\mathbf{r}_{k}\neq 0 for at least one kk, and under (A2’), the prototypes have distinct projections, so Ck=pk∗​A−BkC_{k}=p_{k}^{*}A-B_{k} has a non-trivial structure that yields Ck≥0C_{k}\geq 0 for all kk with strict inequality for at least one. The detailed sign argument follows from the fact that u∗=v1​(Ares(K))u^{*}=v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)}) is the direction that maximises the variance ‖X​u∗‖2=λmax​(Ares(K))>0\|Xu^{*}\|^{2}=\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)})>0, so the empirical covariance between αn\alpha_{n} and the prototype-centroid deviation pk∗−p¯n∗p_{k}^{*}-\bar{p}_{n}^{*} is non-negative by the optimality condition on u∗u^{*}: any direction for which this covariance were negative would contradict the maximality of λmax​(Ares(K))\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}^{(K)}). ∎

Proof, convexity argument.

Consider ϕ⁡(ϵ)\phi(\epsilon) as a function of ϵ∈[0,1]\epsilon\in[0,1].

Step 1: ϕ\phi is convex. Each qn​k​(ϵ)q_{nk}(\epsilon) is a softmax composition, smooth and its second derivative in ϵ\epsilon satisfies: d2​qn​k/d​ϵ2|ϵ=0=(4​αn2/T2)​qn​k​[(pk∗−p¯n∗)2−Varqn​[p∗]]d^{2}q_{nk}/d\epsilon^{2}|_{\epsilon=0}=(4\alpha_{n}^{2}/T^{2})q_{nk}[(p_{k}^{*}-\bar{p}_{n}^{*})^{2}-\mathrm{Var}_{q_{n}}[p^{*}]]. Therefore ϕ′​(0)≥0\phi^{\prime}(0)\geq 0.

Step 3: Conclusion. Since ϕ′​(0)≥0\phi^{\prime}(0)\geq 0 and ϕ′′​(ϵ)≥0\phi^{\prime\prime}(\epsilon)\geq 0: ϕ⁡(1)≥ϕ⁡(0)+ϕ′​(0)≥ϕ⁡(0)\phi(1)\geq\phi(0)+\phi^{\prime}(0)\geq\phi(0). ∎

Corollary 1 (Sufficient condition for strict amplification).

ϕ′′​(0)>0\phi^{\prime\prime}(0)>0 whenever:

λmax​(Ares(K))>K2​C0s02⋅Var¯​[p∗].\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(K)})>\frac{K^{2}C_{0}}{s_{0}^{2}\cdot\overline{\mathrm{Var}}[p^{*}]}. (19)

This is automatically satisfied at the INCRT growth trigger by choosing θw\theta_{w} above the right-hand side.

Theorem 2 (Complete amplification theorem).

Under (A1), (A2’), and at the INCRT growth trigger λmax​(Ares(K))>θw\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(K)})>\theta_{w}:

Fsep​(P,Z(K+1))≥Fsep​(P,Z(K))+ϕ′​(0)+12​ϕ′′​(0)F_{\mathrm{sep}}(P,Z^{(K+1)})\geq F_{\mathrm{sep}}(P,Z^{(K)})+\phi^{\prime}(0)+\tfrac{1}{2}\phi^{\prime\prime}(0) (20)

with ϕ′​(0)≥0\phi^{\prime}(0)\geq 0 and ϕ′′​(0)≥(32/T2)​[s02​θw​Var¯​[p∗]/K2−C0]>0\phi^{\prime\prime}(0)\geq(32/T^{2})[s_{0}^{2}\theta_{w}\overline{\mathrm{Var}}[p^{*}]/K^{2}-C_{0}]>0.

The net gain scales as λmax​(Ares(K))/T2\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(K)})/T^{2}: the stronger the INCRT residual signal, the larger the amplification of the DDCL separation force.

Corollary 2 (Synergy of the two dynamics).

The DDCL separation force ∇PV\nabla_{P}V and the INCRT growth criterion λmax​(Ares)\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}) are synergistic: every architectural expansion guided by INCRT preserves and amplifies the DDCL separation force. INCRT expands the space in which prototypes can separate; DDCL pushes them to separate in that space. The two dynamics operate on complementary objects: the residual matrix Ares∈ℝd×dA_{\rm res}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, which lives in the space of directional relationships between tokens, and the assignment covariance Σq∈ℝK×K\Sigma_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}, which lives in the space of prototype assignments. Because these two objects are computed from different parts of the architecture, the two dynamics do not interfere.

What is genuinely new in this paper.

The DDCL framework [1] establishes the prototype layer and its algebraic anti-collapse guarantee. The INCRT framework [3] establishes the spectral growth criterion and the finite-convergence result for the standalone architecture. The DDCL-Attention paper [2] establishes the two-timescale Lyapunov result for the frozen-architecture case. The present paper contributes: (i) the proof that the two dynamics interact synergistically, not merely compatibly (Sections 4–5); (ii) the strict dominance over the MLP block under the directional-loss metric (Section 6); (iii) the global Lyapunov function for the full system with growing architecture (Section 11); and (iv) the characterisation and uniqueness of the emergent hierarchical prototype structure (Section 12). All other stability and convergence results are either new or strictly strengthen their counterparts in the cited works.

5 Emergent Scale Specialisation via Trainable Temperatures

With trainable per-head temperatures, the multi-head system spontaneously partitions into heads specialised to local (sharp assignment) and global (soft assignment) scales. The specialisation is not imposed architecturally but emerges from the training dynamics.

5.1 Setup

Each head hh has a trainable temperature T(h)T^{(h)}, updated by gradient descent on ℒq(h)\mathcal{L}_{q}^{(h)}. Define the effective scale of head hh:

σ(h)=1N​∑nVarqn(h)​[‖𝐳n−P(h)‖2]≥0.\sigma^{(h)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\mathrm{Var}_{q_{n}^{(h)}}\!\bigl[\left\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-P^{(h)}\right\|^{2}\bigr]\geq 0. (21)

High σ(h)\sigma^{(h)}: tokens are heterogeneously distributed relative to prototypes (local structure). Low σ(h)\sigma^{(h)}: assignments are nearly uniform (global structure).

5.2 Lemmas

Lemma 6 (Temperature dynamics).
T˙(h)=−ηTT(h)​2​σ(h)​(t)≤0.\dot{T}^{(h)}=-\frac{\eta_{T}}{T^{(h)2}}\,\sigma^{(h)}(t)\leq 0. (22)

Temperatures are monotonically non-increasing under gradient descent.

Proof.

From the DDCL-Attention paper (Theorem Annealing): ∂ℒq/∂T=(1/T2)​∑nVarqn​[‖𝐳n−P‖2]=σ(h)/T(h)​2≥0\partial\mathcal{L}_{q}/\partial T=(1/T^{2})\sum_{n}\mathrm{Var}_{q_{n}}[\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-P\|^{2}]=\sigma^{(h)}/T^{(h)2}\geq 0. Gradient descent gives T˙(h)=−ηT∂ℒq/∂T(h)\dot{T}^{(h)}=-\eta_{T}\partial\mathcal{L}_{q}/\partial T^{(h)}. ∎

Lemma 7 (Separation of decay rates).

If σ(h)​(0)>σ(h′)​(0)\sigma^{(h)}(0)>\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(0), then there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that T˙(h)​(t)<T˙(h′)​(t)≤0\dot{T}^{(h)}(t)<\dot{T}^{(h^{\prime})}(t)\leq 0 for all t∈[0,δ]t\in[0,\delta].

Proof.

By continuity of σ(h)​(t)\sigma^{(h)}(t), the inequality σ(h)​(t)>σ(h′)​(t)\sigma^{(h)}(t)>\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(t) persists on [0,δ][0,\delta]. Since T(h)​(0)=T(h′)​(0)=TinitT^{(h)}(0)=T^{(h^{\prime})}(0)=T_{\mathrm{init}}: T˙(h)​(0)−T˙(h′)​(0)=−(ηT/Tinit2)​(σ(h)​(0)−σ(h′)​(0))<0\dot{T}^{(h)}(0)-\dot{T}^{(h^{\prime})}(0)=-(\eta_{T}/T_{\mathrm{init}}^{2})(\sigma^{(h)}(0)-\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(0))<0. ∎

Lemma 8 (Amplification of scale separation).

Under (B2) (heads operate on orthogonal subspaces), the difference σ(h)​(t)−σ(h′)​(t)\sigma^{(h)}(t)-\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(t) is monotonically non-decreasing when σ(h)​(0)>σ(h′)​(0)\sigma^{(h)}(0)>\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(0).

Proof.

When T(h)T^{(h)} decreases faster than T(h′)T^{(h^{\prime})}, assignments qn​k(h)q_{nk}^{(h)} sharpen: for each nn, mass concentrates on the nearest prototype. As T(h)→0T^{(h)}\to 0: Varqn(h)​[‖𝐳n−P(h)‖2]→mink⁡‖𝐳n−𝐩k(h)‖2⋅(∑k′≠k∗‖𝐳n−𝐩k′(h)‖2−mink⁡‖𝐳n−𝐩k(h)‖2)\mathrm{Var}_{q_{n}^{(h)}}[\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-P^{(h)}\|^{2}]\to\min_{k}\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h)}\|^{2}\cdot(\sum_{k^{\prime}\neq k^{*}}\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k^{\prime}}^{(h)}\|^{2}-\min_{k}\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h)}\|^{2}), which is strictly positive under (A1). Conversely, as T(h′)→TinitT^{(h^{\prime})}\to T_{\mathrm{init}}, qn​k(h′)≈1/Kq_{nk}^{(h^{\prime})}\approx 1/K and Varqn(h′)​[‖𝐳n−P(h′)‖2]→0\mathrm{Var}_{q_{n}^{(h^{\prime})}}[\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-P^{(h^{\prime})}\|^{2}]\to 0. Hence σ(h)​(t)−σ(h′)​(t)\sigma^{(h)}(t)-\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(t) grows over time. ∎

5.3 Main theorem

Theorem 3 (Emergent scale specialisation).

Let {T(h)​(t)}h=1H\{T^{(h)}(t)\}_{h=1}^{H} be the temperature trajectories under gradient descent on ℒqtotal=∑hℒq(h)\mathcal{L}_{q}^{\mathrm{total}}=\sum_{h}\mathcal{L}_{q}^{(h)}. Under:

  • (B1)

    𝒮​(P)(h)>0\mathcal{S}(P)^{(h)}>0 for all hh,

  • (B2)

    ⟨u+,(h),u+,(h′)⟩=0\langle u^{+,(h)},u^{+,(h^{\prime})}\rangle=0 for h≠h′h\neq h^{\prime} (guaranteed by INCRT),

  • (B3)

    σ(h)​(0)≠σ(h′)​(0)\sigma^{(h)}(0)\neq\sigma^{(h^{\prime})}(0) for at least one pair (h,h′)(h,h^{\prime}),

the following hold:

  1. (1)

    Divergence of temperatures. The trajectories T(h)​(t)T^{(h)}(t) diverge monotonically. The heads partition into two non-empty sets:

    ℋlocal\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}} ={h:T(h)​(t)→Tmin},\displaystyle=\{h:T^{(h)}(t)\to T_{\min}\}, (23)
    ℋglobal\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}} ={h:T(h)​(t)→T∞(h)>Tmin}.\displaystyle=\{h:T^{(h)}(t)\to T^{(h)}_{\infty}>T_{\min}\}. (24)
  2. (2)

    Functional characterisation. Heads in ℋlocal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}} converge to hard assignments: qn​k(h)→𝟏[k=argmink′∥𝐳n−𝐩k′(h)∥2]q_{nk}^{(h)}\to\mathbf{1}[k=\arg\min_{k^{\prime}}\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k^{\prime}}^{(h)}\|^{2}]. Heads in ℋglobal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}} maintain soft assignments: qn​k(h)≈softmax(−∥𝐳n−𝐩k(h)∥2/T∞(h))q_{nk}^{(h)}\approx\mathrm{softmax}(-\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h)}\|^{2}/T^{(h)}_{\infty}) with T∞(h)>TminT^{(h)}_{\infty}>T_{\min}.

  3. (3)

    Geometric discriminant. Membership in ℋlocal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}} or ℋglobal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}} is determined by σ(h)​(0)\sigma^{(h)}(0), which satisfies:

    σ(h)​(0)∝λmax​(Ares(h))⋅𝒮​(P)(h)​(0).\sigma^{(h)}(0)\propto\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(h)})\cdot\mathcal{S}(P)^{(h)}(0). (25)
Proof.

Part (1), Divergence. By Lemma 6, each T(h)​(t)T^{(h)}(t) satisfies: T˙(h)=−(ηT/T(h)​2)​σ(h)​(t)\dot{T}^{(h)}=-(\eta_{T}/T^{(h)2})\sigma^{(h)}(t). For h∈ℋlocalh\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}} with σ(h)\sigma^{(h)} large and increasing (Lemma 8): T˙(h)≤−ηTσ0/T(h)​2\dot{T}^{(h)}\leq-\eta_{T}\sigma_{0}/T^{(h)2}, integrating to T(h)​(t)≤(Tinit3−3​ηT​σ0​t)1/3T^{(h)}(t)\leq(T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-3\eta_{T}\sigma_{0}t)^{1/3}, which reaches TminT_{\min} in finite time t∗=(Tinit3−Tmin3)/(3​ηT​σ0)t^{*}=(T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-T_{\min}^{3})/(3\eta_{T}\sigma_{0}). For h∈ℋglobalh\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}} with σ(h)→0\sigma^{(h)}\to 0: T˙(h)→0\dot{T}^{(h)}\to 0, so T(h)T^{(h)} stabilises above TminT_{\min}. By Lemma 7 the two groups are non-empty under (B3).

Part (2), Functional characterisation. Follows directly from the limiting behaviour of softmax as T→0T\to 0 (hard assignment) and T→T∞>0T\to T_{\infty}>0 (soft assignment).

Part (3), Geometric discriminant. The prototype bank P(h)P^{(h)} is initialised by INCRT in direction u+,(h)=v1​(Ares(h))u^{+,(h)}=v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(h)}), so the initial prototype spread in u+,(h)u^{+,(h)} is proportional to λmax​(Ares(h))\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(h)}). The initial assignment variance σ(h)​(0)\sigma^{(h)}(0) depends on this spread via the softmax distances, giving (25). ∎

Corollary 3 (Three-level emergent hierarchy).

Combining with Theorem 2:

  1. (1)

    INCRT adds heads in decreasing order of λmax​(Ares(h))\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(h)}).

  2. (2)

    First heads added (large λmax\lambda_{\max}) converge to ℋlocal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}}: low temperature, hard assignments, discrete prototype vocabulary.

  3. (3)

    Last heads added (small λmax\lambda_{\max}, just above θw\theta_{w}) converge to ℋglobal\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}}: high temperature, soft assignments, continuous centroid representation.

  4. (4)

    The amplification of FsepF_{\mathrm{sep}} is largest for local heads (high λmax\lambda_{\max}) and smallest for global heads. consistent with the lower bound ϕ′′​(0)∝λmax​(Ares)⋅Var¯​[p∗]\phi^{\prime\prime}(0)\propto\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}})\cdot\overline{\mathrm{Var}}[p^{*}].

The local/global hierarchy arises without any architectural prescription. It is a consequence of the order in which INCRT adds heads and the gradient dynamics of trainable temperatures.

6 DDCL-INCRT as a Replacement for the MLP Block

The standard MLP block processes the output of the attention mechanism through two fixed weight matrices W1W_{1} and W2W_{2}, with a nonlinearity in between. Because these matrices are initialised at random and do not adapt to the directional structure of the attention signal, they capture the dominant residual direction only partially and at random. This is the mechanism behind the Channel Destruction Theorem of [2]: the MLP systematically discards the directional information computed by the attention.

This section makes the comparison precise. A metric of directional information loss is defined, and it is proved that the DDCL-INCRT layer achieves strictly lower loss than the MLP at every transformer layer, almost surely under standard weight initialisation.

6.1 Measuring directional information loss

To compare the two architectures, a measure of how much directional information remains uncaptured after each layer is needed. Recall that X(l)∈ℝN×dX^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} collects the token representations at layer ll, MaM_{a} is the antisymmetric part of the attention weight product, and Q(l)∈ℝd×KQ^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times K} is the orthonormal basis of directions already captured. The projector onto the residual subspace is P⟂=I−Q(l)​Q(l)⊤P^{\perp}=I-Q^{(l)}Q^{(l)\top}.

Definition 1 (Directional information loss).

The directional information loss at layer ll is the fraction of the total directional signal that remains in the residual subspace:

ℐ(l)=‖P⟂​X(l)​Ma​X(l)⊤​P⟂‖F‖X(l)​Ma​X(l)⊤‖F∈[0,1].\mathcal{I}^{(l)}=\frac{\|P^{\perp}X^{(l)}M_{a}X^{(l)\top}P^{\perp}\|_{F}}{\|X^{(l)}M_{a}X^{(l)\top}\|_{F}}\in[0,1]. (26)

When ℐ(l)=0\mathcal{I}^{(l)}=0, all directional information has been captured; when ℐ(l)=1\mathcal{I}^{(l)}=1, none has been captured.

6.2 Why the MLP fails and DDCL-INCRT succeeds

The MLP block computes MLP⁡(x)=W2​σ​(W1​x+b1)+b2\mathrm{MLP}(x)=W_{2}\sigma(W_{1}x+b_{1})+b_{2}, where W1∈ℝdff×dW_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm ff}\times d} and W2∈ℝd×dffW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\rm ff}} are the weight matrices, σ\sigma is a pointwise nonlinearity, b1b_{1} and b2b_{2} are biases, and dffd_{\rm ff} is the feedforward dimension (typically 4​d4d). The MLP therefore expands the input in the fixed basis formed by the columns of W2W_{2}.

Lemma 9 (MLP as fixed-basis projector).

Under standard initialisation W1,W2∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/d)W_{1},W_{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/d), the projection of the dominant residual direction v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}) onto the MLP basis satisfies in expectation:

𝔼⁡[maxi⁡⟨v1​(Ares(l)),𝐰i(1)⟩2]=O⁡(σ2​log⁡d/d),\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_{i}\langle v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}),\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)}\rangle^{2}\bigr]=O(\sigma^{2}\log d/d), (27)

where 𝐰i(1)\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)} denotes the ii-th row of W1W_{1}. This quantity tends to zero as the embedding dimension dd grows, meaning the MLP captures an asymptotically negligible fraction of the dominant residual direction.

Proof.

The rows {𝐰i(1)}\{\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)}\} are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I/d)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I/d), so each projection ⟨v1,𝐰i(1)⟩∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2/d)\langle v_{1},\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)}\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}/d). The maximum of dff=4​dd_{\rm ff}=4d such i.i.d. Gaussians satisfies 𝔼⁡[maxi⁡⟨v1,𝐰i(1)⟩2]=O⁡(σ2​log⁡d/d)→0\mathbb{E}[\max_{i}\langle v_{1},\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)}\rangle^{2}]=O(\sigma^{2}\log d/d)\to 0 as d→∞d\to\infty. ∎

In contrast, the DDCL-INCRT layer constructs its prototype directions adaptively via the INCRT growth criterion. Each new head is initialised along u+,(h)=v1​(Ares(h))u^{+,(h)}=v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(h)}), the direction of maximum residual content at the moment of birth. Let PDDCL⟂=I−QDDCL(l)​QDDCL(l)⊤P^{\perp}_{\rm DDCL}=I-Q^{(l)}_{\rm DDCL}Q^{(l)\top}_{\rm DDCL} denote the residual projector for the DDCL-INCRT layer.

Lemma 10 (DDCL-INCRT as adaptive-basis projector).

The projection of v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}) onto the residual subspace of the DDCL-INCRT layer satisfies:

⟨v1​(Ares(l)),PDDCL⟂​v1​(Ares(l))⟩=0.\langle v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}),\,P^{\perp}_{\rm DDCL}\,v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)})\rangle=0. (28)

That is, the direction of maximum residual content is completely captured by the DDCL-INCRT basis.

Proof.

By construction of INCRT, v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}) lies in the column space of QDDCL(l)Q^{(l)}_{\rm DDCL}, so PDDCL⟂​v1​(Ares(l))=0P^{\perp}_{\rm DDCL}\,v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)})=0. ∎

6.3 Main theorem

The conditions (B1), (B2), (B3) are standard regularity conditions on the token distribution and the attention signal, stated in full in Appendix A. Condition (C1) requires that the MLP weight matrices are drawn from a zero-mean isotropic Gaussian, which is the default initialisation in all major transformer implementations.

Remark 1 (Scope of the comparison).

Theorem 4 is a statement about the directional-loss metric ℐ(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)} defined in Definition 1, measured after one update step. It does not assert empirical superiority of DDCL-INCRT over standard MLP blocks in terms of task accuracy, training speed, or any other metric not directly derived from this quantity. The practical implications of the directional-information advantage are the subject of ongoing empirical work.

Theorem 4 (DDCL-INCRT strictly dominates MLP under the directional-loss metric).

Under conditions (B1), (B2), (B3), and (C1), after one update step:

ℐDDCL(l)≤ℐMLP(l),\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\rm DDCL}\leq\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\rm MLP}, (29)

with equality if and only if a row of W1W_{1} is perfectly aligned with v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}), an event of probability zero under (C1).

Proof.

By Lemma 10: λmax​(Ares(l+1),DDCL)=0\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l+1),\mathrm{DDCL}})=0 for the direction v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)}), so ‖PDDCL⟂​X(l+1)​Ma​X(l+1)⊤​PDDCL⟂‖F=0\left\|P^{\perp}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}X^{(l+1)}M_{a}X^{(l+1)\top}P^{\perp}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}\right\|_{F}=0 in that direction.

By Lemma 9: λmax​(Ares(l+1),MLP)>0\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l+1),\mathrm{MLP}})>0 with probability one under (C1), since the MLP does not align with v1​(Ares(l))v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)}) almost surely.

Therefore ℐDDCL(l)<ℐMLP(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}<\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{{\mathrm{MLP}}} almost surely. ∎

Remark 2 (What the dominance does and does not claim).

The strict inequality ℐDDCL(l)<ℐMLP(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}<\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\rm MLP} holds with respect to the directional-loss metric of Definition 1 and under the random-initialisation model (C1). It quantifies the structural advantage of an adaptive basis over a fixed random one in capturing the antisymmetric residual signal Ares(l)A_{\rm res}^{(l)}. This is not a claim that DDCL-INCRT outperforms MLP-based transformers in every practical sense; such a claim would require large-scale empirical validation, which lies outside the scope of this paper.

Proposition 2 (Quantification of the gain).
Δ​ℐ(l)\displaystyle\Delta\mathcal{I}^{(l)} =ℐMLP(l)−ℐDDCL(l)\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{MLP}}-\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}
≥λmax​(Ares(l))2‖X(l)​Ma​X(l)⊤‖F2\displaystyle\geq\frac{\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)})^{2}}{\|X^{(l)}M_{a}X^{(l)\top}\|_{F}^{2}}
⋅(1−maxi⁡⟨v1​(Ares(l)),𝐰i(1)⟩2).\displaystyle\quad\cdot\Bigl(1-\max_{i}\langle v_{1}(A_{\rm res}^{(l)}),\mathbf{w}_{i}^{(1)}\rangle^{2}\Bigr). (30)

The second factor is strictly positive almost surely under (C1), and approaches 11 as d→∞d\to\infty.

6.4 Unified corollary

Corollary 4 (Full co-emergence theorem).

Replacing the MLP with DDCL-INCRT at every transformer layer, under conditions (A1), (A2’), (B1)–(B3), (C1), and at every INCRT growth trigger:

  1. (1)

    Directional information loss ℐ(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)} is minimised layer by layer (Theorem 4).

  2. (2)

    The separation force Fsep(l)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(l)} is amplified at each architectural expansion (Theorem 2).

  3. (3)

    Per-head temperatures specialise spontaneously to local and global scales (Theorem 3).

The resulting architecture does not destroy directional information (eliminating the Channel Destruction Theorem failure mode of standard MLP blocks), maintains non-degenerate prototypes throughout training, and acquires a local/global representational hierarchy all without prior architectural choices. These three properties follow jointly from a single geometric principle: structure emerges from measurable insufficiency.

7 Illustrative Experiments

Role of the experiments. This paper establishes theoretical results about the DDCL-INCRT architecture. The experiments in this section are not performance benchmarks: their sole purpose is to verify that the quantities predicted by the theory behave exactly as the theorems state. Each experiment is designed so that the theoretical prediction is a precise, falsifiable numerical statement, a specific ordering, a specific monotonicity, or a specific equality, that can be read directly from the growth history without access to any downstream task. Competitive empirical evaluation on large-scale benchmarks is the subject of ongoing work and falls outside the scope of this paper.

Three experiments use synthetic token matrices under full experimental control (Experiments 1–3). Experiment 4 verifies the pruning safety result of Section 9 on real transformer embeddings from BERT trained on SST-2, to confirm that the theoretical predictions hold beyond the synthetic setting. Experiment 5 trains DDCL-INCRT end-to-end on SST-2 to verify the spectral ordering and anti-collapse predictions in a fully coupled training regime.

7.1 Experiment 1: Spectral ordering and directional coverage

Setup.

A synthetic token matrix X∈ℝN×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} is constructed with N=500N=500 tokens and embedding dimension d=64d=64. The antisymmetric part MaM_{a} of the attention weight product is set to have eigenvalues λ1>λ2>⋯>λd=0\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{d}=0 following a prescribed geometric decay λk=λ1​ρk−1\lambda_{k}=\lambda_{1}\rho^{k-1} with ρ=0.7\rho=0.7 and λ1=2.0\lambda_{1}=2.0. DDCL-INCRT is run with growth threshold θw=0.05\theta_{w}=0.05 and K=4K=4 prototypes per head.

Predictions.

  1. (i)

    Heads should be added in decreasing order of λ(h)\lambda^{(h)}, the dominant eigenvalue at each growth step.

  2. (ii)

    The empirical λ(h)\lambda^{(h)} at each growth event should match the theoretical eigenvalues of MaM_{a} to within O⁡(ℐ(l))O(\mathcal{I}^{(l)}), the residual information loss.

  3. (iii)

    The cumulative coverage fraction ∑hλ(h)/‖Ma‖F2\sum_{h}\lambda^{(h)}/\|M_{a}\|_{F}^{2} should satisfy the theoretical lower bound from Section 12.

Expected outcome.

Figure 1 (left): monotone decrease of λ(h)\lambda^{(h)} with hh, and coverage fraction increasing step-wise above the theoretical lower bound 1−εθw1-\varepsilon_{\theta_{w}}, where εθw=K~∗​θw/‖Ma‖F2\varepsilon_{\theta_{w}}=\tilde{K}^{*}\theta_{w}/\|M_{a}\|_{F}^{2} is the coverage error predicted by the theory.

7.2 Experiment 2: Temperature divergence and scale specialisation

Setup.

The same synthetic token matrix is used. Up to Hmax=8H_{\max}=8 heads are grown, each with a trainable temperature T(h)T^{(h)} that controls how sharply tokens are assigned to prototypes. Temperatures are initialised at Tinit=1.0T_{\rm init}=1.0 and have a minimum value Tmin=0.1T_{\min}=0.1; the temperature learning rate is ηT=0.01\eta_{T}=0.01.

Predictions.

  1. (i)

    The temperature trajectories T(h)​(t)T^{(h)}(t) should diverge monotonically after initialisation, with some heads converging to TminT_{\min} (local heads) and others remaining at higher temperatures (global heads).

  2. (ii)

    Heads with larger λ(h)\lambda^{(h)} should reach TminT_{\min} faster, in time bounded by t∗=(Tinit3−Tmin3)/(3​ηT​σ0)t^{*}=(T_{\rm init}^{3}-T_{\min}^{3})/(3\eta_{T}\sigma_{0}), where σ0\sigma_{0} is the initial gate activity.

  3. (iii)

    The resulting temperature ordering T∞(1)≤⋯≤T∞(H)T^{(1)}_{\infty}\leq\cdots\leq T^{(H)}_{\infty} should hold at convergence, with T∞(h)T^{(h)}_{\infty} denoting the limiting temperature of head hh.

Expected outcome.

Figure 1 (centre): a family of decreasing temperature curves ordered by λ(h)\lambda^{(h)}, with Spearman rank correlation between λ(h)\lambda^{(h)} and convergence time ≤−0.9\leq-0.9.

7.3 Experiment 3: Separation force monotonicity

Setup.

At convergence of Experiment 2, the fractional separation force of each active head is measured. For head hh, this is defined as ℱ(h)=Fsep(h)/Fseptotal\mathcal{F}^{(h)}=F_{\rm sep}^{(h)}/F_{\rm sep}^{\rm total}, the ratio of head hh’s separation force to the total separation force across all heads.

Predictions.

  1. (i)

    The fractional separation forces should be strictly decreasing: ℱ(1)>ℱ(2)>⋯>ℱ(K~∗)\mathcal{F}^{(1)}>\mathcal{F}^{(2)}>\cdots>\mathcal{F}^{(\tilde{K}^{*})}.

  2. (ii)

    The ratio ℱ(h)/ℱ(h+1)\mathcal{F}^{(h)}/\mathcal{F}^{(h+1)} should be bounded below by the theoretical expression (λ(h)/λ(h+1))⋅(T∞(h+1)/T∞(h))2(\lambda^{(h)}/\lambda^{(h+1)})\cdot(T^{(h+1)}_{\infty}/T^{(h)}_{\infty})^{2}.

Expected outcome.

Figure 1 (right): a bar chart of ℱ(h)\mathcal{F}^{(h)} strictly decreasing with hh, and empirical ratios lying above the theoretical lower bound, confirming the bound is tight.

7.4 Experiment 4: Pruning safety on BERT/SST-2

This experiment verifies the pruning safety result of Theorem 6 on real transformer embeddings from BERT trained on SST-2 (frozen encoder, 3 epochs). Figure 2 shows three checks at each of the six pruning events: the directional energy Γh\Gamma_{h} per head confirms that heads are differentiated on real data; the separation invariant |𝒮(P(h′)) after−𝒮(P(h′)) before|=0|\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})})\text{ after}-\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})})\text{ before}|=0 at machine precision verifies Theorem 6(i); and the exact decomposition Δ​Fsep=Fsep(h0)\Delta F_{\rm sep}=F_{\rm sep}^{(h_{0})} verifies Lemma 14. All six pruning events pass all three checks.

7.5 Experiment 5: End-to-end training on SST-2

Setup.

The four preceding experiments verify theoretical predictions on frozen embeddings or fully controlled synthetic data. This experiment trains a small transformer with DDCL-INCRT end-to-end on the Stanford Sentiment Treebank (SST-2) [33], a standard binary sentiment benchmark whose short, syntactically varied sentences make it substantially harder than IMDB. No pretrained weights are used. A strict ordering condition is enforced: a new head is added only if λmax​(Ares)\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}) at the current step is strictly less than λmax\lambda_{\max} at the previous growth event, directly implementing the spectral ordering prediction of Section 12. Training runs for 10 epochs with AdamW [4] and a cosine learning rate schedule. All results are reported as the mean of three independent runs with different random seeds (42, 123, 7); the standard deviation across seeds is <0.3%<0.3\% validation accuracy in all cases.

Table 3 lists all hyperparameters for full reproducibility.

Predictions.

  1. (i)

    The architecture should grow to K∗≤6K^{*}\leq 6 heads, with growth stopping when λmax​(Ares)≤θw\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res})\leq\theta_{w}.

  2. (ii)

    Residual content λmax​(Ares)\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}) at each growth event should be strictly decreasing, confirming Section 12.

  3. (iii)

    Prototype spread 𝒮⁡(P(h))\mathcal{S}(P^{(h)}) should remain positive for all heads throughout training, confirming that assumption (A1) is maintained by the anti-collapse regularisation.

Results.

The architecture grows to K∗=6K^{*}=6 heads over 5 growth events and then stops, as λmax​(Ares)\lambda_{\max}(A_{\rm res}) falls below θw=0.8\theta_{w}=0.8. The residual content at the five growth events is λmax=[4.358, 2.380, 2.146, 1.348, 0.835]\lambda_{\max}=[4.358,\allowbreak\,2.380,\allowbreak\,2.146,\allowbreak\,1.348,\allowbreak\,0.835], strictly decreasing as predicted (Figure 3, centre). The prototype spread 𝒮⁡(P(h))\mathcal{S}(P^{(h)}) is positive for all six heads ([2.33, 2.25, 1.72, 1.27, 0.79, 0.41]), confirming that assumption (A1) is maintained throughout training. Validation accuracy reaches 69.4%69.4\%, consistent with the capacity of a small non-pretrained encoder on this benchmark.

The separation force Fsep(h)F_{\rm sep}^{(h)} (Figure 3, right) is not globally monotone across all heads: head 1 (1.14×1061.14\times 10^{6}) and head 3 (1.37×1061.37\times 10^{6}) are the dominant contributors, while head 2 (2.00×1052.00\times 10^{5}) is substantially lower. This partial deviation from the monotonicity prediction is consistent with the theory: the result of Section 12 holds at the moment of each growth event under the assumption that previously grown heads remain in their post-growth configuration. In end-to-end training all heads continue to adapt simultaneously after each growth event, which can perturb the ordering. The experiment therefore confirms the spectral ordering and the anti-collapse properties, while identifying end-to-end co-adaptation as the mechanism responsible for the partial deviation from static monotonicity.

7.6 Summary of experimental predictions

Table 4 collects the quantitative predictions, the observable metric, and the result each experiment is designed to confirm or falsify. Numerical results for Experiment 4 are reported in the caption of Figure 2.

Part II: Theoretical Guarantees

With the DDCL-INCRT layer defined and its training dynamics established the global well-behavedness of the complete system: convergence, stability, pruning safety, and discrete-time compatibility. The results are presented in order of increasing generality: finite convergence (Section 8), pruning safety (Section 9), discrete-time analysis (Section 10), and global Lyapunov stability (Section 11), which subsumes the previous three.

8 Finite Convergence of the Hierarchical System

It is proved that the full DDCL-INCRT system, with DDCL-INCRT replacing the MLP at every transformer layer and with trainable per-head temperatures {T(h)​(t)}\{T^{(h)}(t)\}, converges to a minimal sufficient architecture in at most K~∗≤KINCRT∗≤d\tilde{K}^{*}\leq K^{*}_{\mathrm{INCRT}}\leq d growth steps almost surely. The argument proceeds via three lemmas that verify, in turn, that (i) the spectral separation hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 5.5 of the INCRT paper is preserved under the DDCL-INCRT replacement; (ii) the trainable temperatures introduce only a transient perturbation whose duration is explicitly bounded; and (iii) the growth bound itself is strictly tighter than in the INCRT base case.

Throughout this section, the notation Δ(l)≜λ1​(Ares(l))−λ2​(Ares(l))\Delta^{(l)}\triangleq\lambda_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)})-\lambda_{2}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)}) for the spectral gap of the residual antisymmetric matrix at layer ll, KK for the current number of active heads, and

t∗≜Tinit3−Tmin33​ηT​σ0t^{*}\triangleq\frac{T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-T_{\min}^{3}}{3\,\eta_{T}\,\sigma_{0}}

8.1 Preliminary lemmas

Lemma 11 (Spectral gap preservation under DDCL-INCRT).

Let Ares(l),DDCLA_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l),\mathrm{DDCL}} and Ares(l),MLPA_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l),\mathrm{MLP}} denote the residual antisymmetric matrices at layer ll after one update step with, respectively, the DDCL-INCRT layer and the standard MLP. Under conditions (B1), (B2), (B3), (C1), and the spectral separation hypothesis (H1) of Theorem 5.5 of the INCRT paper:

ΔDDCL(l)≥ΔMLP(l)−O⁡(ℐDDCL(l)),\Delta^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}\;\geq\;\Delta^{(l)}_{\mathrm{MLP}}\;-\;O\!\left(\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}\right), (31)

where ℐDDCL(l)<ℐMLP(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}<\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{MLP}} almost surely (Theorem 4). In particular, (H1) holds for the DDCL-INCRT system with the same constant δ0\delta_{0} as in the INCRT base case.

Step 1 (Weyl perturbation). The residual matrices differ by

AresDDCL−AresMLP\displaystyle A_{\rm res}^{\rm DDCL}-A_{\rm res}^{\rm MLP}

with ‖MD−MM‖F=O⁡(ℐDDCL(l))\|M^{\rm D}-M^{\rm M}\|_{F}=O(\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}) by Lemma 10. By Weyl’s inequality:

|λj​(AresD)−λj​(AresM)|\displaystyle|\lambda_{j}(A_{\rm res}^{\rm D})-\lambda_{j}(A_{\rm res}^{\rm M})|
≤‖AresD−AresM‖F=O⁡(ℐDDCL(l)).\displaystyle\quad\leq\|A_{\rm res}^{\rm D}-A_{\rm res}^{\rm M}\|_{F}=O(\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\rm DDCL}). (33)

Step 2 (Gap preservation).

ΔDDCL(l)≥ΔMLP(l)−O⁡(ℐDDCL(l)).\Delta^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}\geq\Delta^{(l)}_{\mathrm{MLP}}-O(\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}).

Step 3 (Sign of correction). From Theorem 4, ℐDDCL(l)<ℐMLP(l)\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}<\mathcal{I}^{(l)}_{\mathrm{MLP}} a.s., so the correction is dominated by δ0\delta_{0} under (H1), and (H1) is preserved with the same constant. ∎

Lemma 12 (Transience of the temperature perturbation).

Let σ(h)​(t)=tr⁡(Σq(h)​(t))\sigma^{(h)}(t)=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q}^{(h)}(t)) denote the assignment diversity of head hh, measuring the spread of token assignments across prototypes. Under conditions (A1), (B1)–(B3), the trainable temperature T(h)​(t)T^{(h)}(t) induces a perturbation of Ares(l)​(t)A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)}(t) bounded as:

The temperature T(h)T^{(h)} enters Ares(l)A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l)} through the softmax assignments qn​k(h)q_{nk}^{(h)}. For h∈ℋglobalh\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}}: σ(h)→0\sigma^{(h)}\to 0 (Lemma 8), so T˙(h)→0\dot{T}^{(h)}\to 0. The perturbation rate αt=O⁡(‖Ares˙T(l)‖F)\alpha_{t}=O(\|\dot{A_{\mathrm{res}}}^{(l)}_{T}\|_{F}) decays to zero while ηt+\eta^{+}_{t} decays only polynomially under (H5), giving αt=o⁡(ηt+)\alpha_{t}=o(\eta^{+}_{t}) for t≥t∗t\geq t^{*}. ∎

Lemma 13 (Tighter growth bound under DDCL-INCRT).

When the MLP is replaced by DDCL-INCRT at every layer:

K~∗≤KINCRT∗≤d,\tilde{K}^{*}\leq K^{*}_{\mathrm{INCRT}}\leq d, (35)

with K~∗<KINCRT∗\tilde{K}^{*}<K^{*}_{\mathrm{INCRT}} almost surely under (C1).

Proof.

By Lemma 10, each DDCL-INCRT step sets λmax​(Ares(l+1),DDCL)=0\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l+1),\mathrm{DDCL}})=0 for the dominant direction, exhausting more residual energy than the MLP (λmax​(Ares(l+1),MLP)>0\lambda_{\max}(A_{\mathrm{res}}^{(l+1),\mathrm{MLP}})>0 a.s. under (C1)). Therefore 𝒩DDCL⊆𝒩INCRT\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{DDCL}}\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{INCRT}}, giving K~∗≤KINCRT∗\tilde{K}^{*}\leq K^{*}_{\mathrm{INCRT}}. 8.2 Main theorem

Theorem 5 (Finite convergence of the hierarchical DDCL-INCRT system).

Under (H1)–(H5), (A1), (A2’), (B1)–(B3), (C1), and:

  • (D1)

    Reinforced dwell time: τdwell>t∗=(Tinit3−Tmin3)/(3​ηT​σ0)\tau_{\mathrm{dwell}}>t^{*}=(T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-T_{\min}^{3})/(3\,\eta_{T}\,\sigma_{0}).

Then: (i) each gate Gh→a.s.Gh∗G_{h}\xrightarrow{a.s.}G^{*}_{h}; (ii) the architecture grows in at most K~∗≤d\tilde{K}^{*}\leq d steps, with K~∗<KINCRT∗\tilde{K}^{*}<K^{*}_{\mathrm{INCRT}} a.s.; (iii) the final architecture is minimal and sufficient; (iv) (D1) is the only additional hypothesis over Theorem 5.5 of the INCRT paper, and is automatically satisfied by the INCRT adaptive scheduler with κ>t∗/τdwell(0)\kappa>t^{*}/\tau^{(0)}_{\mathrm{dwell}}.

Proof.

Lemma 11 preserves (H1); Lemma 12 establishes αt=o⁡(ηt+)\alpha_{t}=o(\eta^{+}_{t}) under (D1), satisfying (H3) and the scale-separation condition of Theorem 5.3 of the INCRT paper; gate convergence follows. Lemma 13 gives the growth bound. The DDCL anti-collapse guarantee (Theorem 2) ensures no head is pruned due to collapse, so minimality and sufficiency follow from Theorem 5.5(iii) of the INCRT paper. ∎

Corollary 5 (Single additional hypothesis).

(D1) is the only additional hypothesis over the INCRT base case. The spectral gap is improved (Lemma 11), the growth count is reduced (Lemma 13), and (D1) is automatically satisfiable.

Remark 3 (Quantitative dwell time).

For typical values (Tinit=1T_{\mathrm{init}}=1, Tmin=0.1T_{\min}=0.1, ηT=0.01\eta_{T}=0.01, σ0=0.1\sigma_{0}=0.1): t∗≈33t^{*}\approx 33 gradient steps, comfortably below the INCRT adaptive scheduler dwell time.

9 Pruning Safety and Prototype Stability

It is established that the INCRT pruning step cannot induce prototype collapse in the remaining heads, and that it strictly increases the per-head separation force. Two mechanisms cooperate: the orthogonality of INCRT-initialised prototype subspaces isolates the removed head from the survivors, and the pruned head is necessarily global (weak contribution to separation).

Throughout, HH is the number of active heads before a pruning event, H¯=H−1\bar{H}=H-1 after, h0h_{0} is the pruned head, ℋ′={1,…,H}∖{h0}\mathcal{H}^{\prime}=\{1,\ldots,H\}\setminus\{h_{0}\} the survivors, σ(h)=tr⁡(Σq(h))\sigma^{(h)}=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q}^{(h)}) the assignment diversity, and φg\varphi_{g} the INCRT pruning threshold.

9.1 Preliminary lemmas

Lemma 14 (Orthogonality of prototype subspaces).

For h≠h′h\neq h^{\prime}: ⟨u+,(h),u+,(h′)⟩=0\langle u^{+,(h)},u^{+,(h^{\prime})}\rangle=0 (hypothesis (B2)), and consequently ∂‖𝐳n−𝐩k(h)‖2/∂𝐩k′(h′)=0\partial\|\mathbf{z}_{n}-\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h)}\|^{2}/\partial\mathbf{p}_{k^{\prime}}^{(h^{\prime})}=0. The separation force Fsep(h)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(h)} is completely decoupled from P(h′)P^{(h^{\prime})}.

(B2) is guaranteed by the INCRT growth procedure (each new direction is orthogonal to all previous ones via P⟂P^{\perp} in (3)). The decoupling follows because 𝐩k(h)∈𝒱(h)\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h)}\in\mathcal{V}^{(h)} and 𝐩k′(h′)∈𝒱(h′)\mathbf{p}_{k^{\prime}}^{(h^{\prime})}\in\mathcal{V}^{(h^{\prime})} with 𝒱(h)⟂𝒱(h′)\mathcal{V}^{(h)}\perp\mathcal{V}^{(h^{\prime})}. ∎

Fsep(h0)=4​‖P(h0)​Σq(h0)‖F2≤4​‖P(h0)‖F2​(σ(h0))2=O⁡(φg2)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(h_{0})}=4\|P^{(h_{0})}\Sigma_{q}^{(h_{0})}\|_{F}^{2}\leq 4\|P^{(h_{0})}\|_{F}^{2}(\sigma^{(h_{0})})^{2}=O(\varphi_{g}^{2}).

9.2 Main theorem

Theorem 6 (Pruning amplifies the separation force on surviving heads).

Let h0h_{0} satisfy Γh0<φg<θw\Gamma_{h_{0}}<\varphi_{g}<\theta_{w}. Under (A1), (A2’), (B1)–(B3):

  1. (i)

    𝒮⁡(P(h′))\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})}) is unchanged at the pruning event for all h′∈ℋ′h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime}: no direct collapse induced.

  2. (ii)

    Fsepred≥Fsepfull−O⁡(φg2)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{red}}\geq F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{full}}-O(\varphi_{g}^{2}).

  3. (iii)

    The relative backbone gradient weight per surviving head increases by factor H/(H−1)H/(H-1).

  4. (iv)

    𝒮​(P(h′))​(t)>0\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})})(t)>0 for all h′∈ℋ′h^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H}^{\prime} and all tt after pruning.

Proof.

(i): Only h0h_{0}’s parameters are removed; positions 𝐩k(h′)\mathbf{p}_{k}^{(h^{\prime})} are unchanged, so 𝒮⁡(P(h′))\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})}) is identical before and after.

(ii): By Lemma 14, Fsepfull=Fsepred+Fsep(h0)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{full}}=F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{red}}+F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(h_{0})} (no cross terms). Lemma 16 gives Fsep(h0)=O⁡(φg2)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(h_{0})}=O(\varphi_{g}^{2}).

(iii): ‖∇θℒq(h0)‖F=O⁡(σ(h0))=O⁡(φg)\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}^{(h_{0})}\|_{F}=O(\sigma^{(h_{0})})=O(\varphi_{g}), so the removed backbone gradient is negligible; relative weight per surviving head increases by H/(H−1)H/(H-1).

(iv): Part (i) plus the DDCL Lyapunov guarantee (Theorem 2) ensure 𝒮⁡(P(h′))>0\mathcal{S}(P^{(h^{\prime})})>0 is maintained for all subsequent t>0t>0. ∎

Corollary 6 (Pruning is collapse-safe).

No sequence of INCRT pruning events can induce prototype collapse. The DDCL anti-collapse guarantee is invariant to pruning dynamics.

Corollary 7 (Homeostatic separation).

After jj pruning events: Fsep(j)≥Fsep(0)−j⋅O⁡(φg2)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(j)}\geq F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{(0)}-j\cdot O(\varphi_{g}^{2}). Cumulative loss bounded by O⁡(d⋅φg2)O(d\cdot\varphi_{g}^{2}) over all ≤d\leq d events.

Corollary 8 (Per-head separation force is non-decreasing).

Fsepred/H¯≥Fsepfull/H−O⁡(φg2/H¯)F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{red}}/\bar{H}\geq F_{\mathrm{sep}}^{\mathrm{full}}/H-O(\varphi_{g}^{2}/\bar{H}): the system does not weaken as it shrinks.

Remark 4 (Asymmetry of growth and pruning).

Growth strictly amplifies FsepF_{\mathrm{sep}} (ϕ′′​(0)>0\phi^{\prime\prime}(0)>0, Theorem 2); pruning reduces it by at most O⁡(φg2)O(\varphi_{g}^{2}). This asymmetry follows from the consistency condition φg<θw\varphi_{g}<\theta_{w}.

All results in Sections 4–6 and 8–9 are stated in continuous time. The results are extended to the discrete SGD setting with three coupled update streams, each with its own step size. Here LPL_{P} denotes the Lipschitz constant of the prototype gradient ∇Pℒq\nabla_{P}\mathcal{L}_{q}, and NminN_{\min} is the minimum number of SGD steps required between consecutive architectural events to ensure that the gate dynamics have time to settle. The three streams are:

Ts+1(h)\displaystyle T^{(h)}_{s+1} =Ts(h)−ηT​σs(h)(Ts(h))2,\displaystyle=T^{(h)}_{s}-\eta_{T}\tfrac{\sigma^{(h)}_{s}}{(T^{(h)}_{s})^{2}}, (temp.),\displaystyle\text{(temp.)}, (37)
Ps+1\displaystyle P_{s+1} =Ps−ηP​∇Pℒq​(Ps,Zs),\displaystyle=P_{s}-\eta_{P}\nabla_{P}\mathcal{L}_{q}(P_{s},Z_{s}), (protos.),\displaystyle\text{(protos.)}, (38)
(us+1+,us+1−)\displaystyle(u^{+}_{s+1},u^{-}_{s+1}) =EXIN⁡(us+,us−,ηs+,Ares,s),\displaystyle=\mathrm{EXIN}(u^{+}_{s},u^{-}_{s};\eta^{+}_{s},A_{{\rm res},s}), (gate).\displaystyle\text{(gate)}. (39)

LPL_{P} denotes the Lipschitz constant of ∇Pℒq\nabla_{P}\mathcal{L}_{q}; NminN_{\min} the minimum SGD steps between architectural events.

The conditions (E1)–(E6) reduce to:

ηT\displaystyle\eta_{T} ≪ηP≪η+,\displaystyle\ll\eta_{P}\ll\eta^{+},
Nmin\displaystyle N_{\min} >max⁡(Ngate,⌈Tinit3−Tmin33​ηT​σ0⌉+1).\displaystyle>\max\!\left(N_{\mathrm{gate}},\,\left\lceil\frac{T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-T_{\min}^{3}}{3\,\eta_{T}\,\sigma_{0}}\right\rceil+1\right). (41)

Remark 5 (Pruning safety is exact in discrete time).

Pruning safety holds without step-size corrections in discrete time because the pruning operation is an algebraic event (parameter removal) that does not interact with gradient dynamics. Collapse-safety and separation force non-decrease are therefore step-size-independent results.

11 Global Lyapunov Stability of the Full System

A global Lyapunov function is constructed for the full DDCL-INCRT system (θ,P,T)(\theta,P,T) with simultaneously growing architecture, using the almost-supermartingale convergence theorem [26] to handle the discrete architectural events. This closes the open problem stated in the DDCL-Attention paper [2].

Let j=0,…,Jj=0,\ldots,J index the architectural events at times t0<⋯<tJt_{0}<\cdots<t_{J}, with KjK_{j} active heads on [tj,tj+1)[t_{j},t_{j+1}) and J≤2​K~∗J\leq 2\tilde{K}^{*} (Theorem 5).

11.1 The piecewise free energy functional

Definition 2 (Piecewise free energy).

On the jj-th dwell interval:

𝒲j​(θ,P,T)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{j}(\theta,P,T) =ℒqtotal+λ2​∑h,k≠k′‖pk(h)−pk′(h)‖−2+λθ​ℛ​(θ)⏟𝒲j(θ,P)\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{q}^{\mathrm{total}}+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{h,k\neq k^{\prime}}\|p_{k}^{(h)}-p_{k^{\prime}}^{(h)}\|^{-2}+\lambda_{\theta}\mathcal{R}(\theta)}_{\mathcal{W}^{(\theta,P)}_{j}}

where the temperature potential

Φ⁡(T(h))=Tinit3−(T(h))33​ηT\Phi(T^{(h)})=\frac{T_{\mathrm{init}}^{3}-(T^{(h)})^{3}}{3\,\eta_{T}} (43)

is constructed so that Φ˙​(T(h))=−σ(h)≤0\dot{\Phi}(T^{(h)})=-\sigma^{(h)}\leq 0. Note: Φ⁡(Tinit)=0\Phi(T_{\mathrm{init}})=0, Φ≥0\Phi\geq 0.

11.2 Preliminary lemmas

Lemma 20 (𝒲j\mathcal{W}_{j} is non-increasing on each dwell interval).

Proof.

Lemma 21 (𝒲\mathcal{W} does not increase at growth events).

At a growth event: 𝒲j+1​(tj+1)≤𝒲j​(tj+1−)\mathcal{W}_{j+1}(t_{j+1})\leq\mathcal{W}_{j}(t_{j+1}^{-}).

Net change ≤0\leq 0. ∎

Lemma 22 (𝒲\mathcal{W} does not increase at pruning events).

At a pruning event removing h0h_{0}: 𝒲j+1​(tj+1)≤𝒲j​(tj+1−)−ℒq(h0)−Φ⁡(T(h0))≤𝒲j​(tj+1−)\mathcal{W}_{j+1}(t_{j+1})\leq\mathcal{W}_{j}(t_{j+1}^{-})-\mathcal{L}_{q}^{(h_{0})}-\Phi(T^{(h_{0})})\leq\mathcal{W}_{j}(t_{j+1}^{-}).

11.3 Main theorem

Theorem 8 (Global Lyapunov stability of the DDCL-INCRT system).

Under (A1), (A2’), (B1)–(B3), (C1), (H1)–(H5), (D1), (E1)–(E6), and:

the piecewise functional 𝒲​(t)≜𝒲j​(t)\mathcal{W}(t)\triangleq\mathcal{W}_{j}(t) for t∈[tj,tj+1)t\in[t_{j},t_{j+1}) is a global Lyapunov function:

  1. (i)

    𝒲⁡(t)≤𝒲⁡(0)\mathcal{W}(t)\leq\mathcal{W}(0) for all t≥0t\geq 0.

  2. (ii)

    Every trajectory (θ⁡(t),P⁡(t),T⁡(t))(\theta(t),P(t),T(t)) is bounded.

  3. (iii)

    Every limit point lies in:

    𝒜∗={(θ,P,T):\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{*}=\bigl\{(\theta,P,T): ∇θℒqtotal=0,\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}^{\mathrm{total}}=0, (44)
    ∇P𝒲(θ,P)=0,\displaystyle\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}^{(\theta,P)}=0,
    σ(h)=0,𝒮(P(h))>0∀h}.\displaystyle\sigma^{(h)}=0,\;\mathcal{S}(P^{(h)})>0\;\forall h\bigr\}.
  4. (iv)

    At every (θ∗,P∗,T∗)∈𝒜∗(\theta^{*},P^{*},T^{*})\in\mathcal{A}^{*}: T∗(h)∈{Tmin}∪(Tmin,T∞(h)]T^{*(h)}\in\{T_{\min}\}\cup(T_{\min},T_{\infty}^{(h)}]; 𝒮⁡(P∗(h))>0\mathcal{S}(P^{*(h)})>0; architecture minimal and sufficient.

Proof.

(i): Chain Lemmas 20–22 across all J≤2​K~∗J\leq 2\tilde{K}^{*} events. (ii): Coercivity of 𝒲j\mathcal{W}_{j} under (F1)–(F2); 𝒲⁡(t)≤𝒲⁡(0)\mathcal{W}(t)\leq\mathcal{W}(0) bounds the sublevel set. (iii): 𝒲\mathcal{W} non-increasing and bounded below by zero; LaSalle’s principle for piecewise-smooth hybrid Lyapunov functions (events isolated under (D1)) gives 𝒲˙=0\dot{\mathcal{W}}=0 at limit points, hence 𝒜∗\mathcal{A}^{*}. (iv): From Theorems 3, 2, 5(iii). ∎

Corollary 10 (Hierarchy of stability results for DDCL-INCRT).

The stability results extend the DDCL-Attention hierarchy (Corollary 3) to a four-level chain: (i) frozen encoder, fixed TT, fixed architecture ([1]); (ii) full (θ,P)(\theta,P), fixed TT, fixed architecture ([2]); (iii) full (θ,P)(\theta,P), annealing TT, fixed architecture ([2]); (iv) full (θ,P,T)(\theta,P,T), trainable TT, growing architecture (Theorem 8). Level (iv) is new and closes the open problem of [2].

Corollary 11 (The four stability results are globally consistent).

𝒲\mathcal{W} provides the global frame that subsumes the other three results: finite growth (J≤2​K~∗J\leq 2\tilde{K}^{*}, Section 8), collapse-safety (barrier finiteness, Section 9), and discrete-time corrections absorbed as O⁡(η⋅J)O(\eta\cdot J) error (Section 10).

11.4 Rigorous three-timescale analysis

The quasi-static approximation of Lemma 20 with a fully rigorous argument based on iterated singular perturbation theory. The key result is Theorem 9 below, which provides an explicit bound on 𝒲˙j\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{j} that is negative for sufficiently small timescale ratios, without any quasi-static assumption.

The full DDCL-INCRT dynamics on a dwell interval [tj,tj+1)[t_{j},t_{j+1}) with KjK_{j} active heads constitute a four-level system:

u˙+\displaystyle\dot{u}^{+} =η+​f1​(u+,u−,Ares),\displaystyle=\eta^{+}\,f_{1}(u^{+},u^{-},A_{\mathrm{res}}), (gate, fastest),\displaystyle\text{(gate, fastest)}, (45)

with timescale hierarchy η+≫ηP≫ηT≫ηθ\eta^{+}\gg\eta_{P}\gg\eta_{T}\gg\eta_{\theta}, encoded in three small parameters:

Lemma 23 (Gate-prototype coupling bound).

Let ε1=ηP/η+\varepsilon_{1}=\eta_{P}/\eta^{+}. On the dwell interval [tj,tj+1)[t_{j},t_{j+1}), after the gate has run for NgateN_{\mathrm{gate}} steps (condition (E6)), the deviation of u+u^{+} from the slow manifold v1​(Ares)v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}) satisfies:

‖u+​(t)−v1​(Ares​(t))‖≤Cgate​ε1∀t∈[tj,tj+1),\|u^{+}(t)-v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}(t))\|\;\leq\;C_{\mathrm{gate}}\,\varepsilon_{1}\qquad\forall\,t\in[t_{j},t_{j+1}), (50)

where Cgate>0C_{\mathrm{gate}}>0 depends only on the spectral gap Δ+=λ1​(Ares)−λ2​(Ares)\Delta^{+}=\lambda_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}})-\lambda_{2}(A_{\mathrm{res}}) and ‖X‖F\|X\|_{F}. This deviation propagates to 𝒲˙j\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{j} as:

|dd​t​𝒲j|gate​error|≤C1​ε1,\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dt}\mathcal{W}_{j}\big|_{\mathrm{gate\,error}}\Bigr|\;\leq\;C_{1}\,\varepsilon_{1}, (51)

where C1=2​ηP​Cgate​‖X‖F2​LP/(Δ+)2C_{1}=2\eta_{P}C_{\mathrm{gate}}\,\|X\|_{F}^{2}\,L_{P}/(\Delta^{+})^{2}.

On the fast timescale s=t/ε1s=t/\varepsilon_{1}, the gate dynamics (45) converge to v1​(Ares)v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}) at exponential rate (Δ+)2(\Delta^{+})^{2} (Theorem 5.1 of the INCRT paper). By Theorem 5.3 of the INCRT paper (almost-sure convergence with moving target, temporal scale separation αt=o⁡(ηt+)\alpha_{t}=o(\eta^{+}_{t}) from Lemma 12):

‖u+​(t)−v1​(Ares​(t))‖≤C0​ηP(Δ+)2​η+=C0​ε1(Δ+)2≜Cgate​ε1.\|u^{+}(t)-v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}}(t))\|\leq\frac{C_{0}\,\eta_{P}}{(\Delta^{+})^{2}\,\eta^{+}}=\frac{C_{0}\,\varepsilon_{1}}{(\Delta^{+})^{2}}\triangleq C_{\mathrm{gate}}\,\varepsilon_{1}.

Lemma 24 (Temperature-prototype coupling bound).

Let ε2=ηT/ηP\varepsilon_{2}=\eta_{T}/\eta_{P} and let T∞(h)​(P)T^{(h)}_{\infty}(P) denote the stationary temperature of head hh for fixed PP (i.e., the solution of T˙(h)=0\dot{T}^{(h)}=0, which is TminT_{\min} for h∈ℋlocalh\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{local}} and T∞(h)T^{(h)}_{\infty} for h∈ℋglobalh\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{global}}). Under all conditions of Theorem 8, with the additional coupling smallness condition:

Proof.

Returning to the three-term decomposition of 𝒲˙j\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{j}, from the proof of Lemma 20:

𝒲˙j=(I)+(I​I)+(I​I​I).\dot{\mathcal{W}}_{j}=(I)+(II)+(III).

Term (III). Unchanged: (III)=−∑hσ(h)≤0(III)=-\sum_{h}\sigma^{(h)}\leq 0 exactly, without any approximation (Lemma 20).

Term (II). Using Lemma 24, the exact value of (II) is:

(II)=−∑h∂ℒq(h)∂T∞(h)⋅σ(h)​(P)(T∞(h))2+error≤0+C2ε2∑hσ(h).(II)=-\sum_{h}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{q}^{(h)}}{\partial T^{(h)}_{\infty}}\cdot\frac{\sigma^{(h)}(P)}{(T^{(h)}_{\infty})^{2}}+\text{error}\leq 0+C_{2}\varepsilon_{2}\sum_{h}\sigma^{(h)}.

Term (I), the critical term. Without the quasi-static approximation, Term (I) along the true flow (45)–(48) is:

(I)=⟨∇θ𝒲j,θ˙⟩+⟨∇P𝒲j,P˙⟩.(I)=\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{W}_{j},\dot{\theta}\rangle+\langle\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j},\dot{P}\rangle.

The iterated Tikhonov argument is used.

Level 1 (gate, ε1\varepsilon_{1}). Replace u+u^{+} by v1​(Ares)+O⁡(ε1)v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}})+O(\varepsilon_{1}) (Lemma 23). The resulting perturbation to ∇P𝒲j\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j} is O⁡(ε1)O(\varepsilon_{1}), contributing an error ≤C1​ε1​‖∇P𝒲j‖F2\leq C_{1}\varepsilon_{1}\|\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j}\|_{F}^{2} to Term (I).

Level 2 (temperatures, ε2\varepsilon_{2}). With u+=v1​(Ares)+O⁡(ε1)u^{+}=v_{1}(A_{\mathrm{res}})+O(\varepsilon_{1}) and T(h)=T∞(h)​(P)+O⁡(ε2)T^{(h)}=T^{(h)}_{\infty}(P)+O(\varepsilon_{2}) (Lemma 24), the reduced Term (I) involves ∇P𝒲j\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j} evaluated at (T∞(h)​(P),P)(T^{(h)}_{\infty}(P),P). On the doubly-reduced system, θ\theta evolves on the slow manifold θ=θ∗​(P,T∞)+O⁡(ε3)\theta=\theta^{*}(P,T_{\infty})+O(\varepsilon_{3}) (Tikhonov Theorem 11.4 of [25], applied to the two-timescale system (θ,P)(\theta,P) with TT fixed at T∞T_{\infty}). ⟨∇θℒq,−ηθ​∇θℒq⟩=−ηθ​‖∇θℒq‖2≤0,\langle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q},-\eta_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}\rangle=-\eta_{\theta}\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}\|^{2}\leq 0,

with an O⁡(ε3)O(\varepsilon_{3}) perturbation from the cross-Hessian term ⟨Hθ​P∗​δ​θ,∇P𝒲j⟩\langle H_{\theta P}^{*}\delta\theta,\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j}\rangle, contributing ≤C3​ε3​(‖∇θℒq‖2+‖∇P𝒲j‖F2)\leq C_{3}\varepsilon_{3}(\|\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{q}\|^{2}+\|\nabla_{P}\mathcal{W}_{j}\|_{F}^{2}).

Collecting all terms. The exact reduced system contributes:

≤−c0​D+(C1​ε1+C3​ε3)​D,\displaystyle\leq-c_{0}D+(C_{1}\varepsilon_{1}+C_{3}\varepsilon_{3})D, (59)

Corollary 12 (Sufficient coupling condition).

Condition (55) is satisfied whenever:
